name: Monotone Monochrome Matrices (Easy Version)
description: This is the easy version of the problem. The difference between the versions is that in this version, the constraints on $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ are smaller. You can hack only if you solved all versions of this problem. A monochrome matrix of size $$$n \times n$$$ is a matrix of $$$n$$$ rows and $$$n$$$ columns, where each cell is colored either black or white. Let the color of cell $$$(r,c)$$$ in a monochrome matrix $$$C$$$ be denoted as $$$C[r,c]$$$. Let's call such a matrix $$$C$$$ monotone if it satisfies the following condition: There exist no two rows $$$1 \le i \lt j \le n$$$ and two columns $$$1 \le k \lt l \le n$$$ that satisfy the following three conditions: $$$C[i,k]=C[j,l]$$$; $$$C[j,k]=C[i,l]$$$; $$$C[i,k] \neq C[j,k]$$$. There is a monochrome matrix $$$M$$$ of size $$$n \times n$$$, where all cells are initially white. Please solve $$$q$$$ queries of the following kind: $$$r\;c$$$: Change the color of the cell $$$(r,c)$$$ in $$$M$$$ to black . Then, determine if $$$M$$$ is monotone or not. For each query, it is guaranteed that the color of the cell $$$(r,c)$$$ was white before the query. Do note that the updates are persistent. In other words, the change in color from one query affects the later queries as well.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^3$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 25\,000$$$, $$$1 \le q \le \min(n^2,200\,000)$$$). Each of the $$$q$$$ following lines contains two integers $$$r_i$$$, $$$c_i$$$ denoting the $$$i$$$-th query ($$$1 \le r_i,c_i \le n$$$). For each query, it is guaranteed that the color of the cell $$$(r,c)$$$ was white before the query. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$25\,000$$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$q$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$200\,000$$$.
output_specification: For each query, output " YES " or " NO " on a separate line based on the answer of the query. You can output the answer in any case. For example, the strings " yEs ", " yes ", and " Yes " will also be recognized as positive responses.

approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2202G1 — Monotone Monochrome Matrices (Easy Version) [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
